articles.title: A Palm Beach mansion bought for $21.9 million with funds linked to a former CIA official's $194 million fraud scheme has resold for $24 million; the property was among luxury assets the official agreed to forfeit
articles.summary: A luxury mansion in Palm Beach, Florida, that was bought using money stolen through a major government fraud scheme has been sold for $24 million.
articles.body: A luxury mansion in Palm Beach, Florida, that was bought using money stolen through a major government fraud scheme has been sold for $24 million. The fraud was carried out by a former CIA official who admitted to stealing nearly $194 million from the US government. The waterfront property at 1430 South Ocean Boulevard was sold on 16 November 2026, according to real estate records cited by The Real Deal. The latest sale represents an increase from the $21.9 million paid for the mansion just two years earlier by a company linked to the former government employee. The mansion was among several expensive assets seized by the US government after former federal employee David T. Nichols was convicted. Nichols pleaded guilty in 2025 to defrauding the federal government of approximately $194 million.The $194 Million Government Fraud SchemeThe United States Department of Justice reported that David T. Nichols, a former CIA employee who later worked as a contractor for the Defense Intelligence Agency, admitted to carrying out a large and long-running fraud scheme. Over several years, Nichols used his position to steal money intended for sensitive government operations. He diverted approximately $194 million from US government accounts for his personal use. "Nichols abused his position of trust with the federal government to steal nearly $200 million of taxpayer money, which he laundered through a sophisticated network of shell companies and luxury purchases," U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia Jessica D. Aber said in a Justice Department press release detailing the guilty plea. The scheme involved creating false invoices and misusing government payment systems. Nichols used the stolen money to fund an expensive lifestyle. His purchases included several properties, luxury cars and high-value investments across the United States.Palm Beach Mansion Among Forfeited AssetsThe Palm Beach mansion was one of the main properties bought using money from the fraud. Located in one of South Florida's most exclusive neighbourhoods, the waterfront home was purchased for $21.9 million in 2024. The money used for the purchase was traced directly to Nichols' fraudulent activities. After his arrest, Nichols pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering charges. He also agreed to a wide-ranging asset forfeiture order, which required him to give up property and other assets bought with money from the $194 million scheme. The assets included the Palm Beach mansion, other properties and millions of dollars held in cash and securities. The US Marshals Service took control of the seized properties and prepared them for sale. The money raised from selling these assets was intended to help repay the government agencies affected by the fraud. The forfeiture was part of the government's effort to recover money that Nichols had taken through the scheme and used to purchase expensive assets.The $24 Million ResaleAfter the mansion was seized, the federal government put the South Ocean Boulevard property on the market. Its location in Palm Beach and its range of luxury features attracted interest from potential buyers. According to The Real Deal's report on the transaction, the buyer paid $24 million for the mansion. The sale was completed on 16 November 2026. The transaction marks another step in the government's efforts to recover assets linked to the fraud. The property sold for $2.1 million more than the $21.9 million paid in 2024. The increase also reflects the value of the property in Palm Beach's high-end real estate market during the period between the two transactions. The money recovered from the mansion's sale, along with funds raised through the sale of other forfeited assets, will be returned to the US Treasury to help offset the nearly $200 million lost through the fraud. Nichols is currently serving a lengthy federal prison sentence for his crimes. articles.body: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in a Chicago suburb is facing additional charges, including terrorism and armed violence, police said on Wednesday (local time).A grand jury indicted Alexandros Paporakis, from Palatine, on November 5 on six counts of terrorism, two counts of armed violence and two counts of attempted terrorism. He also faces nine additional counts of making terrorist threats.The indictment includes weapons-related charges, including possessing a firearm without a serial number and failing to have a police-issued identification card.Following his arrest, Paporakis was initially charged with making a terrorist threat and illegally possessing a riflePolice have not explained why they delayed announcing the indictment.A judge has ordered Paporakis to remain in custody, describing him as a threat to the community. He is scheduled to appear in court on Thursday for his arraignment.Paporakis's lawyer, Fedor Kozlov, told The Associated Press that his client still intends to plead not guilty to the charges.The alleged attack planAuthorities allege that Paporakis planned to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, on October 11, the first day of the festival of Navaratri. His co-workers at a Taco Bell alerted police after he reportedly told them he planned to “kill Indian people”. Officers arrested him that afternoon. He initially faced charges of making a terrorist threat and illegally possessing a rifle.According to prosecutors, Paporakis identifies as a white supremacist and neo-Nazi. He allegedly wrote a document detailing his fantasies about murdering non-white people. A search of his home uncovered a rifle, ammunition, a tactical vest and a patch displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism.Hindu community raises concerns The foiled attack sparked alarm among Chicago's Hindu community and South Asian leaders, who linked the threat to rising racist rhetoric against their community. US Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was at the targeted temple on the day of the planned attack, had called on authorities to charge Paporakis with a hate crime. articles.title: Progressives face accusations of racism over attacks on Hakeem Jeffries as he seeks speakership
articles.summary: James Carville and strategist Yemisi Egbewole criticized the far left's attacks on Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as House Democrats nominated him for speaker on Wednesday.
articles.body: Democratic strategists Yemisi Egbewole and James Carville took aim at Rep. Hakeem Jeffries’ progressive House critics after Democrats nominated him for speaker on Wednesday. Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said in an interview with Talking Points Memo that Jeffries would have "a relatively short rope to show that kind of urgency" as speaker. Jayapal said she wanted his help to secure votes for Medicare for All. She later clarified on X that she meant "a short window to act" and condemned the use of lynching imagery to intimidate anyone. Egbewole, who served as chief of staff to the Biden White House press office, pointed to a racial slur Palestinian journalist Rula Jebreal used against Jeffries while criticizing his support for Israel. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Egbewole said the far left had dismissed Jeffries’ record as House minority leader and urged his critics to work with him. "There’s something particularly ugly about the way the far left talks about Jeffries, calling him an ‘AIPAC monkey’ and dismissing his work as minority leader," she said. "They don’t have the votes to block his speakership, let alone elect someone else. Yet rather than work with him, they continue to mock him. I'd hope they wake up, see the writing on the wall, and consider a plan to work with our future speaker." FOLLOW THE LEADER: DEMOCRATS FACE PARTY BATTLE AS DIVISIONS DEEPEN Jayapal did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital about her "short rope" remark. Egbewole declined to address Jayapal's wording. Carville described the progressive movement as insular, saying its acceptance of political allies depended on whether it considered them part of the group. "I find that whole, you know, progressive whole thing very exclusionary in nature," Carville said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "They only want you if they think you’re one of them, you know. I’m not a fan." CHARLAMAGNE BLASTS AOC FOR ‘BEATING AROUND THE BUSH,’ PRESSES PROGRESSIVES ON BACKING HAKEEM JEFFRIES Carville also challenged progressives critical of Jeffries to put up their own candidate for speaker. He said organizing behind someone would give the public a chance to weigh in on what progressives wanted. "Get a candidate, whoever that candidate is, get behind that candidate and take your case to the people," Carville said. CNN contributor and conservative commentator Shermichael Singleton told CNN's Jake Tapper on Tuesday that personal attacks on Jeffries echoed racial language he had heard on the far right. "This is a moment that we should all celebrate," he said. "Instead, because of political differences, they’re attacking him and calling him out of his name, and it is no different to me than the White supremacists on my side who have used racial tropes to describe Black people." Singleton's fellow panelist, Democratic strategist Paul Begala, also described Jayapal’s "short rope" remark as racist. SENATE DEM CHALLENGING SEN CHUCK SCHUMER FOR LEADERSHIP POST BACKS HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR HOUSE SPEAKER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Several incoming House Democrats had withheld their support for Jeffries while seeking commitments on their legislative priorities. No challenger emerged for the Democratic nomination. If elected by the full House on Jan. 3, the New York Democrat would become the first Black speaker in U.S. history.

articles.title: Trump and Putin to meet one-on-one in China Thursday
articles.summary: US and Russia leaders meet in China amid efforts to resolve Ukraine crisis and enhance post-war security guarantees.
articles.body:
Washington, DC, USA – United States President Donald Trump is set to hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, a US official tells Al Jazeera.

The two presidents last met in Alaska in August 2025 for high-stakes negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, but failed to reach a settlement.

The US official said on Wednesday that, in addition to the president’s engagements in China, American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to meet with Ukrainian officials and European partners in Berlin on Thursday to develop post-war security guarantees and a comprehensive economic recovery plan for Kyiv.

“The Berlin meetings and President Trump’s engagements in China are part of a coordinated diplomatic effort,” the official said.

“President Trump remains committed to ending the fighting and the tremendous human suffering, while helping establish the conditions for a sovereign, secure and prosperous Ukraine.”

On Thursday, Trump and Putin are also scheduled to join their Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, for an unprecedented trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen, marking the first-ever gathering of the leaders of the world’s three major powers.

articles.title: In her first all-hands meeting, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress promises salary hikes to 49,000 employees; tells staff: Make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about...
articles.summary: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress used the opening minutes of her first all-hands meeting to talk about money.
articles.body: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress used the opening minutes of her first all-hands meeting to talk about money. She spoke to staff on Wednesday, a week after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. Kress told employees to expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of the usual schedule, according to remarks reviewed by Wired. "So I'm here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp," Kress said.The promise covers a workforce of nearly 49,000 people, who are now working without the founder who ran Nvidia for 33 years.Salary was the top question Nvidia employees sent in before the all-handsKress said about 700 questions were submitted ahead of the meeting, and compensation came up more than anything else. The next most common request was for more transparency from the board.That second ask is easy to understand. Huang resigned on November 12 amid allegations of extramarital affairs. They reportedly include two with Nvidia employees and one with Alice Huang (no relation), a businesswoman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. China has denied any espionage operation. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to probe whether Huang's conduct compromised national security or company secrets. Huang is due to testify before Congress on December 1.Huang's quarterly town halls were a big draw inside the company, and details rarely leaked. Wednesday's meeting broke both patterns.Nvidia board shuts the door on a Jensen Huang returnOpening Tuesday's earnings call, board chair Harvey Jones said the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."Kress has backed that line. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen. And that is our statement and what the board has decided to do," she said. She added that the focus is now on growing the business for employees, customers and shareholders.Outside the company, the push for a comeback is still going. Thousands of employees have reportedly lobbied for Huang's reinstatement. An online petition backed by Elon Musk, Garry Tan and Tim Sweeney has drawn close to 200,000 supporters. President Donald Trump has said he "would not mind" a return.Huang left the door open too. In a post on X on Tuesday, he admitted to "serious mistakes" in his personal life and promised to cooperate with the board's investigation. He also said he would be "honored" to return if the board felt it was best for shareholders, employees, the company and America.Instead, the board has hired search firm Heidrick & Struggles to look at internal and external candidates. On prediction market Kalshi, Arm CEO Rene Haas leads at 25%, followed by Nvidia's Ian Buck at 17%. Huang sits at 9%.Holding on to talent is now Nvidia's top priority, says KressInvestors fear a brain drain. Many of Nvidia's senior engineers are already wealthy, and some stay for the mission Huang drove rather than the paycheck. On the earnings call, a Bank of America Securities analyst asked about retention. Kress said stabilising the employee ranks is "probably the most important thing" leadership is thinking about."We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment," she said.The numbers give her room to spend. Third-quarter revenue more than doubled to $115.8 billion, and data centre revenue rose 110% to $107.6 billion. Profit hit a record $65.3 billion, and Nvidia expects $130 billion in the fourth quarter. Shares rose about 5% on Wednesday. Even so, the company is still worth roughly $2 trillion less than at its October peak.Cofounder Chris Malachowsky joined Kress for a short Q&A and took the culture question. He said he, Huang and the other cofounders thought putting values on posters was "nonsense," because culture shows up in how people behave and work together."We're going to be fine," he said. December's early raises are Nvidia's way of making sure its people stay long enough to see if he's right.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: A Connecticut employee was fired after coworkers noticed a marijuana smell near her car, though no one saw her use drugs at work; 10 years later, a court upheld a $62,530 award for disability discrimination
articles.summary: A suspicion at work has sparked a legal battle spanning 10 years, after a Connecticut worker was fired over reports of the smell of marijuana near her
articles.body: A suspicion at work has sparked a legal battle spanning 10 years, after a Connecticut worker was fired over reports of the smell of marijuana near her parked car. Two other employees smelled the odor, but neither saw her smoke, had marijuana or appeared impaired at work. Almost a decade after the incident, the Connecticut Appellate Court has upheld a ruling that her employer, Charter Communications, discriminated against her because of her mental disability. The Nov. 17, 2026, ruling upholds a $62,530 compensation award to the former employee, Latoya Council, and has drawn renewed attention to disability rights and workplace drug policies.How an incident at work led to dismissalAccording to the ruling in Charter Communications, LLC v. Commission on Human Rights & Opportunities, from the Connecticut Appellate Court, council started as a strategic accounts coordinator for the company in August 2014. The incident that finally cost her her job occurred on June 8, 2016. During a break Council went to her car to check on an oil problem. Two co-workers stopped to help and told police they could smell marijuana coming from the vehicle.Neither fellow employee saw Council smoking or in possession of marijuana and no smoke was seen coming from the car. The matter was then brought to management’s attention. Council admitted to using marijuana in the last month during an internal investigation, but said she had not used it at work or on company property.The case turned into a medical diagnosisIn May 2016, the Connecticut Appellate Court described Council’s diagnosis of chronic post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). After consulting with medical professionals, she was also recommended for Connecticut’s medical marijuana program. On June 9, 2016, the company’s human resources department received medical documentation confirming her diagnosis and referral for PTSD. The following day, the employer ordered Council to take an oral saliva drug test. She was fired for testing positive for marijuana on June 15, which allegedly violated the company’s drug-free workplace policy. The Council then challenged the termination, claiming her firing was disability discrimination under Connecticut law.Why the employer’s explanation was rejectedEventually, the case went to the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, where a human rights referee considered the circumstances of her termination. The referee concluded in May 2023 that Charter Communications discriminated against Council based on her mental disability and ordered the company to pay her $62,530. In a separate reimbursement order, the employer was also ordered to pay the state $9,646 for unemployment compensation and dependency allowances.A key factor was the changing reasons given by the company for the termination. In the case, the Connecticut Appellate Court ruled that the employer’s initial rationale for its actions was based on Council’s purported violation of its drug policy, but then it switched to concerns about Council’s tardiness and her alleged representation about her medical marijuana paperwork. The referee also rejected the Council’s claims that he had used marijuana on company premises or while working, finding no credible evidence to support these claims.Appellate Court upholds finding of discriminationCharter Communications appealed the commission’s ruling, but the Superior Court upheld the finding of disability discrimination in November 2024. The company appealed again. On November 17, 2026, the Connecticut Appellate Court affirmed the lower court’s judgment and rejected the employer’s arguments.The judges said the company had only been confirmed of the Council’s PTSD diagnosis six days before she was dismissed. They also found enough evidence to support the conclusion that the employer’s stated reason for termination was a pretext for discrimination. The decision reaffirms the importance of differentiating between legitimate enforcement of workplace policies and decisions that are tainted by an employee’s disability. Council has won a major legal battle over a 2016 workplace incident with the $62,530 compensation payout upheld.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
articles.summary: This comes after Brand's wife shared a message from him in which he claimed his innocence.
articles.body:
Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

There was no immediate comment from Google when approached by BBC News.

On Sunday, his wife Laura had shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a handwritten message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.

Brand's message prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against him, said she found the message shared on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme this week.

She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised media outlets earlier on Wednesday for playing extracts of the message, saying they should not have "amplified" his words.

Speaking to LBC, she described Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

In 2023, YouTube suspended Brand's channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy", shortly after he was accused of rape and sexual assaults between 2006 and 2013.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site.

Meanwhile, his social media accounts on Meta platforms - Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

articles.title: Oyster photocard holders’ personal data accessed in TfL breach
articles.summary: Names, addresses, dates of birth and security answers were accessed, Transport for London says.
articles.body:
The personal details of about 265,000 Oyster photocard customers have been accessed in a cyber breach, Transport for London (TfL) has said.

Names, email and home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and security questions and answers were compromised after "suspicious activity" was detected on the photocard website on Monday.

TfL said it took the photocard system off line to limit access and had notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

It said no passwords, bank or payment card details or journey information were compromised.

The photocard website remains offline, meaning customers cannot apply for or renew a photocard online until it is restored as an investigation continues.

TfL said customers who needed to renew their photocard or discuss their journey history could contact customer services on 0343 222 1234.

"Customers with Oyster photocards can continue to travel and we hope to restore services as quickly as possible."

It is the second time in just over two years the system had been taken down because of a cyber incident.

In September 2024, a cyber attack on TfL forced it to suspend new photocard applications for more than two months. TfL said at the time that about 5,000 customers had been contacted over possible access to their bank details, but the BBC later revealed that the data of about 10 million people had been stolen.

The ICO cleared TfL of wrongdoing over its handling of that breach.

articles.title: US Defence Secretary Hegseth reveals military partnership on Venezuela trip
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth says the agreement will include joint training and intelligence sharing with the Venezuelan military.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth has announced a new agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.

The Pentagon chief made a surprise visit to the Venezuelan capital of Caracas on Wednesday, becoming the latest in a series of high-level officials under US President Donald Trump to travel to the South American country.

During his stop, Hegseth revealed that the deal would include intelligence sharing and joint training for the two countries’ militaries.

“We see this as a reestablishment of our defence partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries,” he said.

Their shared aim would be “to stabilise Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all”, Hegseth added.

Hegseth was hosted by interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who has led the government since her swearing-in on January 5. His trip was not previously announced by the Pentagon.

The Trump administration has exerted heavy influence over Rodriguez and her government after abducting former President Nicolas Maduro during a military attack on January 3.

Rodriguez was previously Venezuela’s vice president. Trump has justified the attack as a law enforcement effort designed to force Maduro to “stand trial on American soil”, charging him with weapons- and drug-related crimes.

After the operation, Trump also said he planned to “run” Venezuela, and he told The Atlantic magazine that Rodriguez could “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she refuses to comply with US demands.

Since then, he has worked with the Venezuelan government to extract concessions on US priorities such as energy development and military cooperation.

Critics have accused the US of reducing Venezuela to a vassal state and exploiting its resources while leaving Maduro’s government largely intact.

Under Maduro, the Venezuelan state was accused of human rights abuses including torture, arbitrary imprisonment and extrajudicial killings.

Still, Trump has held up Venezuela as a model he would like to see replicated in other countries, like Iran and Cuba.

In Wednesday’s remarks, Hegseth said that the South American country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner”.

Rodriguez hailed the agreement as a “resumption of the technical-military relationship between both countries”, and she expressed hope that their cooperation could be “brought to its highest possible level”.

Hegseth is also set to meet with officials in Colombia later on Wednesday as part of a trip to the region.

Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora said on Tuesday that the US would deliver a C-130 Hercules military aircraft, as the US steps up military involvement across Latin America.

Hegseth has faced pressure to step down from his role, following a midterm election in which the US-Israel war on Iran contributed to Republican losses across the country.

A key member of Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth has championed the war, as well as efforts to weaken rules of engagement designed to limit civilian casualties.

Hegseth narrowly avoided a recent impeachment effort in the US Congress this month. The sponsor of that effort, outgoing Republican US Representative Thomas Massie, cited the Iran war as well as a campaign of military strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels off the coast of Latin America.

The boat-strike campaign has killed an estimated 244 people and has been denounced as extrajudicial killings by legal experts.

articles.title: Newly released videos show men prosecutors say directed London arson attacks in real time
articles.summary: Videos made public Tuesday night show what federal prosecutors say are men gathered around a map of London directing arson attacks in real time against targets in the city earlier this year.
articles.body: Videos made public Tuesday night show what federal prosecutors say are men gathered around a map of London directing arson attacks in real time against targets in the city earlier this year. Prosecutors filed three clips in the Southern District of New York overnight as part of a court fight over jail restrictions for one of the defendants, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi. Al-Saadi was arrested in New York City in May. He is also one of the men alleged to be involved in a plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, in September. According to prosecutors, he used calls with family members while in federal custody, to pass coded messages to his co-defendants in the run-up to the Fairford plot. In one clip, men look at a map of London. “We need to get focused on London,” one says. Another clip shows an individual throwing what looks like a firebomb into a building. Prosecutors say the clip captures a call during an attack on a London synagogue. In the longest clip, which runs 2 minutes and 6 seconds, one man sits behind a laptop while two others stand beside large screens mounted on a wall. A man repeatedly asks to see what’s happening on the other end of the call. “Your camera is off. Show me your camera,” he says. Near the end of the clip, he says, “Cut, cut cut. Well done.” Prosecutors say the call took place during an April arson attack targeting a site linked to a Jewish charity in London. In an exclusive interview with NBC News, Jamie McDonald, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, said the footage illustrates how people overseas can recruit and pay others to carry out attacks and direct them remotely. “It’s probably the worst of the gig economy that you’re seeing come to life here over the last six to nine months,” McDonald said. The eight-count superseding indictment names al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani. Prosecutors alleged the three acted on behalf of a network that included Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), both of which the United States has designated as foreign terrorist organizations. NBC News reached out to Iran’s mission to the United Nations in New York for comment on the videos and the allegations on the indictment. Al-Saadi has pleaded not guilty. Mohajeri and al-Hassani remain at large. It is unclear who recorded the clips, who appears in them or what is happening on the other end of the call. In the indictment, prosecutors identify al-Saadi and al-Hassani in a still from one of the recordings, which they say was made by Mohajeri. An attorney for al-Saadi declined comment on Wednesday. Prosecutors allege the network was behind a series of attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the United States, in addition to a “September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed,” according to a Department of Justice statement. Iran’s embassy in London rejected suggestions that Tehran was linked to the plot. “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot,” Blanche said. Prosecutors cited the videos in arguing that al-Saadi should remain subject to communications restrictions in jail. McDonald said investigators tracked the calls and information from them to piece together the timeline from conversations in June and July to preparations in August and the thwarted plot in September.

articles.title: A Portland architect spent three years building a four-level forest home shaped like a bouquet of flowers; the completed 3,700-square-foot property has circular windows, curved ceilings and a $2.888 million asking price
articles.summary: A Portland architect has spent three years creating a four level forest home shaped like a bouquet of flowers, and it is now on the market for $2.888
articles.body: A Portland architect has spent three years creating a four level forest home shaped like a bouquet of flowers, and it is now on the market for $2.888 million. Designed by Robert Oshatz, the 3,700 square foot residence at 216 NW Royal Blvd in Portland’s West Hills features circular windows, curved wood ceilings, disappearing glass walls, and an indoor elevator, according to Realtor.com and Zillow.The home is the first completed property in a planned collection of five homes sharing 90,000 square feet of forested acreage. Oshatz, an apprentice of Frank Lloyd Wright Jr., envisioned the group as a bouquet of flowers, with each residence designed to feel distinct while belonging to the same sculptural landscape.A home built like a sculptureThe house was designed to feel more like a piece of art than a conventional residence. Its steel framed structure supports curved wood ceilings, rounded windows, and glass walls that can disappear to connect the interior with the surrounding forest.Listing agent Terry Sprague described the architect as someone whose designs stand apart from commoditised architecture, as per the reports. He compared Oshatz to Andy Warhol and Peter Max, saying that every wall and window in the home functions as a sculpture. The design also uses glass placed in specific ways to create rainbows inside the home. Sprague said the architect built prisms into the structure, allowing light to move through the space in different ways throughout the day.Four levels of living spaceThe property has four bedrooms and four bathrooms across its 3,700 square feet. Zillow lists the home as having five stories, with an elevator providing access to all four levels. The main level includes a living room, dining room, kitchen, and one bedroom. The upper level contains the primary bedroom, while the lower level includes additional bedrooms, a family room, and an office.The home also includes a wood burning fireplace, a kitchen island, and two attached garage spaces. Its layout is designed to balance privacy with open, light filled living areas.A modern treehouse in the forestThe property sits on a wooded, sloped lot and offers territorial and tree views. Realtor.com described the home as feeling like a modern treehouse because it is cantilevered out toward the view.The outdoor space includes more than 3,000 square feet of covered porches and walkways. These areas are designed for entertaining and relaxation, but they also reinforce the connection between the home and the forest around it.The setting is part of what makes the property distinctive. Rather than building a conventional house on a flat lot, the architect used the terrain and trees to shape the experience of living there.A collection still taking shapeThe completed home is one of five planned residences on the site. Four additional lots are still build ready, and the listing suggests they could be sold to the buyer of the first home or developed separately.Oshatz is locally known for organic designs, including the Wilkinson Residence, the Rosenthal Residence, and the Fennell Residence. The new project represents a continuation of that approach, with homes intended to feel integrated with their natural surroundings.The listing agent said the architect, who is over 80, wanted to complete this home as part of a lifelong vision. The idea was to create a legacy collection that could inspire future custom builds.Who the home may attractSprague believes the residence may appeal to buyers looking for a second or third home. He noted that baby boomers remain a major segment of high end buyers, particularly those seeking a pied a terre in a scenic location.The home is listed at $2,888,000, or $781 per square foot, according to Zillow. The listing was posted on October 31, 2026, and had already drawn more than 3,500 views and 166 saves within five days.For a buyer who values architecture, privacy, and a connection to nature, the property offers something unusual. articles.title: Venezuela a ‘compliant security partner,’ Hegseth says as he announces military deal with Caracas
articles.summary: The US has signed a new agreement to reestablish military ties with Venezuela more than 10 months after toppling its leader, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said.
articles.body: The United States has signed a new agreement to reestablish military ties with Venezuela more than 10 months after toppling its leader in a military raid, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced during his first trip to the South American nation on Wednesday. “Venezuela has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner,” Hegseth said outside the US Embassy in Caracas. The Pentagon chief described the deal as “historic,” saying it would allow American and Venezuelan forces to train together and share intelligence, defense equipment and other capabilities. He insisted that the partnership would not be “cosmetic” and would require defense and security reforms in Venezuela to modernize its military and eliminate “persistent threats” to both nations. The timeline and scope of the deal remain unclear. The Defense Department has not responded to questions about the agreement or Hegseth’s trip, nor did it provide a daily schedule for the secretary on the day of his visit. Hegseth appeared to have signed the agreement earlier at the Venezuelan presidential palace with Defense Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez, according to footage broadcast on state TV. In a televised meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez, Hegseth said the US looks forward to deepening their defense cooperation “to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders.” Rodriguez said their renewed “technical-military cooperation” is meant to confront common threats and make the region safer. Both Hegseth and Rodriguez underscored their countries’ remarkable turn in relations since the US captured Venezuela’s authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro on January 3. “The weight of this moment does not escape me,” Hegseth said outside the embassy. “Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible.” Rodriguez said, “We have turned very difficult and very harsh moments for our people … into an extraordinary space for cooperation and the mutual benefit of our countries.” Since Maduro’s capture, the US has been working with the acting Venezuelan government on the country’s democratic transition and political reconciliation. Rodriguez has met just about every demand from Washington, including releasing hundreds of political prisoners and making it easier for US companies to invest in the country. Wednesday’s military deal is the latest effort by the Trump administration to bolster security cooperation with Latin American countries with the aim of combating what it calls “designated terrorist organizations” in the region. Hegseth traveled to Colombia later on Wednesday and was expected to discuss security ties and deliver military equipment, according to the Colombian defense minister. That visit comes amid a New York Times report that said Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella this week rejected a US plan for joint anti-crime operations on Colombian soil. A source from Colombia’s Ministry of Defense told CNN that while the government supports increased military cooperation and the intelligence sharing to combat drug cartels and terrorist organizations, it cannot greenlight operations involving foreign forces on the ground, as this requires legislative authorization. Hegseth is also expected to travel to Ecuador and Honduras as part of a tour of Latin America.

Florio understands that to exist in the mainstream sports media, he must conform to certain views. He isn't alone. Bill Simmons and Le Batard are the same way. articles.title: 72-year-old Palestinian woman shot and killed by Israeli settlers near newly established outpost
articles.summary: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot and killed by Israeli settlers in front of her home in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, according to Palestinian officials and eyewitnesses.
articles.body: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot and killed by Israeli settlers in front of her home in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, according to Palestinian officials and eyewitnesses. Fadda Fuhaidat was shot in the head after midnight near the city of Jericho, where Israeli settlers took over eight Palestinian homes two weeks ago. Fuhaidat’s 19-year-old granddaughter, Nagham, told CNN the Israeli settlers have been harassing residents in the area since moving in. The incident on Tuesday began when settlers illegally drove into Area A in the West Bank, which is territory where Israeli civilians are prohibited from entering. But how the shooting unfolded is in dispute and remains under Israeli police investigation, as well as a review from Israel Defense Forces (IDF) commanders. According to Nagham, a group of armed settlers came toward their neighborhood and began firing indiscriminately late Monday evening. Six Palestinians were shot and injured, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry. Nagham said her mother called her husband, Arafat, and asked him to come help. Arafat sped over and hit the settlers’ car by accident, Nagham said. As Arafat stepped out of his car, he was shot in the leg and required medical attention, she said. When Fuhaidat heard gunshots, she ran into the street to see what was happening. A bullet struck her in the back of the head, Nagham said, killing her in front of her home. According to an Israeli military official, a Palestinian car struck the vehicle with Israeli settlers, sparking an argument that quickly escalated. Several additional Israelis and Palestinians arrived at the scene, the official said. As Palestinians threw stones at the Israelis, the official said Israeli settlers fired shots at the Palestinians. articles.title: Japan scrambles fighter jets after Russian aircraft breach airspace amid rising Pacific tensions
articles.summary: Suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Okinoshima, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned of instability at the Quad Leaders Summit.
articles.body: Japan scrambled fighter jets early Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace, prompting a rapid military response ahead of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's warning of rising global instability during the Quad Leaders’ Summit in Manila. Hours later, President Donald Trump had also joined Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the summit, where the leaders voiced opposition to actions threatening regional peace and stability. "We strongly oppose any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability," the leaders said in a joint statement later released by the White House. TRUMP KICKS OFF HIGH-STAKES ASIA TRIP WITH XI, PUTIN MEETINGS LOOMING ON WORLD STAGE On Wednesday, two U.S. military officials confirmed to Fox News that the aircraft carrier USS George Washington was departing the Middle East for the Pacific. Sen. Mazie Hirono, D-Hawaii, questioned acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao Tuesday about the lack of aircraft carriers in the Pacific, noting that three carrier strike groups had been deployed to the Middle East. "There are none in the Indo-Pacific area when we are looking at China, not to mention North Korea and especially what China may have in mind," Hirono said. "See, this is stretching and stressing our resources. You can't take away the strike group out of the Indo-Pacific." The Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace northwest of Okinoshima, an island in southwestern Japan's Fukuoka Prefecture, at about 4:07 a.m. local time Nov. 17, according to Japan's Defense Ministry. Fighter jets from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force's Western Air Defense Force were scrambled to issue warnings and take other measures, the ministry said in a statement posted on X. The first suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace at approximately 4:07 a.m. and remained for three minutes. A second aircraft entered the same area at approximately 4:09 a.m. and departed three minutes later. THREE MANILA MOMENTS THAT GIVE TRUMP MOMENTUM GOING INTO TALKS WITH CHINA Japan's Defense Ministry said the aircraft traveled through the Tsushima Strait and passed between Japan's Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before continuing into the Pacific Ocean. "In response, the Self-Defense Forces scrambled fighter jets from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s Western Air Defense Force to issue notifications and warnings and take other measures," the Ministry of Defense said. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tokyo lodged a strong protest with Moscow and demanded measures to prevent further airspace violations. The incidents "not only constitute a grave infringement upon Japan’s sovereignty but also pose a threat to our security. They are entirely unacceptable," Koizumi said. This came as Takaichi warned of growing instability in the international order and promised a bigger role for Japan in maintaining regional security. CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS "While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play a more proactive role," Takaichi said during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila. Takaichi emphasized Japan's commitment to maintaining an international order based on freedom, openness and the rule of law while strengthening cooperation with Southeast Asian nations. "Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific," Trump had also said ahead of the Quad meeting. The leaders had expressed "grave concerns" about economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions, and outlined plans for a joint military exercise involving maritime patrol aircraft in 2027. KIM JONG UN'S NUCLEAR BUILDUP SPARKS 'SERIOUS CONCERN' AHEAD OF TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT The airspace incursion comes amid broader security concerns across the Indo-Pacific, where Japan and its regional partners have increasingly monitored Russian and Chinese military activity. On Tuesday, South Korea’s air force also scrambled fighter jets as multiple Russian military aircraft had entered the country’s air defense identification zone, according to the Ministry of National Defense. Otherwise, Japan's relations with Moscow have deteriorated since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, with Tokyo joining Western allies in imposing sanctions on the Kremlin. The two countries are also locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over islands north of Japan's northernmost main island of Hokkaido. Russia administers the islands, which Japan claims as its Northern Territories. articles.title: Prince Harry says he’d return to the military to face Russia if needed
articles.summary: Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the US government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump administration’s stance and that of the American people.
articles.body: Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the US government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump administration’s stance and that of the American people. Harry, a British Army veteran who returned to his home country last summer after six years in California, also said he believes Britain has been in conflict with Russia for the past decade and that he is ready to serve in the military once again if he is called upon to do so. The comments came in an interview with The Daily Telegraph that took place last weekend during Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the full-scale Russian invasion. The newspaper published a story about the interview on Wednesday and is scheduled to release the full interview in a podcast that will be posted at midnight London time (7 p.m. Eastern Time). “I think there’s been a big separation between what American society feel regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in this case an administration, that was perhaps thinking about it differently,” Harry said. Harry traveled to Ukraine last weekend to meet with athletes who are preparing to take part in the 2027 Invictus Games, the Paralympic-style competition he founded to inspire wounded veterans. Next year’s games will take place in Birmingham, England. The prince is not a working member of the royal family and traveled to Ukraine as a private citizen. Harry said now is the time for Britain and its allies to double their support for Ukraine to ensure that it defeats Russia at a time when Moscow is trying to stir up divisions within European society. British intelligence and military officials are increasingly warning about sabotage, disinformation campaigns and other so-called hybrid attacks carried out by Russian operatives to destabilize Western societies. “I think the threat has been there and been consistently there for the last 15 years,” Harry said. “Just because there’s not drones, bullets and rockets flying at us, that doesn’t mean that we’re not at war. I feel like we’ve been at war for the last decade.” Harry, who was deployed to Afghanistan twice during his military career, said veterans should be ready to serve again. “If the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel,” he said.

articles.title: Vincent van Gogh painting sells for $190 million, smashing auction record
articles.summary: A Vincent van Gogh masterwork shattered the artist’s auction record just days after a previous owner’s heirs claimed it was sold “under duress” amid Nazi persecution.
articles.body: Just days ago, the sale of a vibrant Vincent van Gogh masterwork painted at the end of the artist’s life was thrown into chaos after heirs of a previous owner claimed it was sold “under duress” amid Nazi persecution. On Wednesday evening, it sold for over $190 million at a Sotheby’s sale in New York, shattering the public auction record for Van Gogh’s work. The week leading up to the blockbuster evening sale of “Châtaigniers en fleurs” was filled with twists and turns until the end. The unnamed heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher who lived in Berlin in the 1930s, claimed the painting had only been sold because of financial difficulties their family faced during Nazi rule. Sotheby’s and the seller, the family of late Argentinian businessman Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his art patron wife Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, both released statements indicating they were taking the matter seriously and were open to dialogue, though the auction house said its provenance research did not match the assertion. Then, on Tuesday, Sotheby’s announced it had reached an agreement with Fischer’s heirs, without disclosing more about the terms. On Wednesday night, a three-minute bidding battle pushed the price far past Van Gogh’s previous record of $117.2 million. The record-setting Van Gogh artwork, which depicts a burst of chestnut trees in the village of Auvers-sur-Oise, where the artist spent his final months after he was released from a psychiatric facility, had not been viewed publicly in half a century. The Blaquier-Arrieta family did not loan their artworks to museums, so many of the 12 lots from Wednesday’s sale have been rarely seen in recent decades. Resultingly, the collection had achieved “legendary mythical status,” according to Sotheby’s Europe chair Helena Newman. “It’s one of the greatest remaining collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art in private hands,” Newman told CNN in September, referring to the group of artworks as “a mini Musée d’Orsay.” Cézanne’s “Arlequin,” for example, is the only example of the artist’s Harlequin series not held by a museum. It sold for over $111 million at Wednesday’s auction, taking the total for the collection’s 12 paintings to almost $412 million. The sale also included works by artists including Edgar Degas and Camille Pissarro. Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s “En Canot (Jeune fille à la barque)” and Claude Monet’s “Le Jardin des Tuileries” were among the other top lots, fetching $27.5 million and $20.23 million, respectively. This year’s marquee November auctions, held across the New York headquarters of Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Phillips and Bonhams, are expected to generate around $2.4 billion in sales. Earlier this week, Christie’s saw a new record set for the work of Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky, whose “Betonte Ecken” — once sold by the Guggenheim for just $62,000 — fetched $85.8 million. Elsewhere, Roy Lichtenstein’s “Reflections on Painter and Model” sold for $24.7 million and one of late Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama’s “Infinity Net” paintings sold for a record $15.1 million on Monday. On Tuesday, just hours before a planned auction, Christie’s postponed the sale of a Frida Kahlo artwork previously reported as missing from a museum in Mexico City. In a statement, a spokesperson for the auction house said the painting had been withdrawn “for further research,” adding: “We look forward to selling this work at a later date.” This story was updated with additional details from the auction.

articles.title: Migrant boat capsizes off Senegal, leaving at least one dead
articles.summary: Incident comes days after another boat capsized in Senegalese waters, and Spain declared a migration emergency.
articles.body:
A small boat carrying migrants and refugees has capsized off the coast of Yenne in western Senegal, killing at least one person.

Local officials told the AFP news agency that the pirogue-type flat-bottomed boat struck a rocky area and washed ashore overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday.

A survivor of the shipwreck who was questioned by the gendarmerie said that there were about 100 people on board the boat, including five women, according to a local elected official.

Yenne Mayor Massamba Mbengue and local firefighters said that one body was recovered, while two other local sources put the body count at two.

Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said that the incident “occurred around 2:00am [02:00 GMT]. Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach”.

The boat washed up on the beach in a dilapidated state, according to eyewitnesses.

A gendarmerie commander sorted items that were found on the boat, including water sachets and personal belongings.

Eight identity documents, several mobile phones and a school enrolment document belonging to a high school student from Kabrousse, in Senegal’s south, were also discovered, according to the local official.

The official said Yenne has become a migration embarkation point, with smugglers coming to the village to recruit boat pilots.

The latest incident comes just 10 days after a shipwreck off the coast of the northwestern town of Thieppe killed 43 people, in one of the deadliest migration disasters in Senegal’s history.

Human rights group Action for Human Rights and Friendship (ADHA) in Senegal called on the government to conduct a parliamentary inquiry into the tragedy.

In a statement released at the time, ADHA denounced a “lack of lasting results” to reduce migrant deaths at sea.

Spain declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands on November 10 after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.

Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on November 14.

That broke the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.

Most migrants arriving in El Hierro depart from West Africa, often from Senegal, hoping to reach mainland Europe.

Last month, Spain deported more than a dozen of the 80,000 people who entered its North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco over 48 hours in late July.

At least 100 people died during the mass crossing into the autonomous city, which covers just 18.5 square kilometres (7.1sq miles) and has a population of about 80,000.

articles.title: Crew unaware of risks before Bayesian yacht accident, say investigators
articles.summary: The vessel sank off the coast of northern Sicily, killing seven people including British tech tycoon Mike Lynch.
articles.body:
The crew of the Bayesian superyacht did not know about a critical safety risk that left it vulnerable in powerful winds before it sank off the coast in northern Sicily coast, killing seven people, British investigators say.

British tech tycoon Mike Lynch, 59, and his daughter Hannah, 18, were among seven people who died when the vessel sank on 19 August 2024 .

The sinking of the Bayesian unfolded with "extraordinary speed" when a violent downburst of freak hurricane-force winds knocked it onto its side in less than 15 seconds, the UK's Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) final report said.

Safety information provided to the crew did not identify this type of risk, the MAIB said.

'For two seconds I lost my baby in the sea' - Sicily yacht survivor

Tributes paid to 'UK's greatest tech entrepreneur'

"It was very dynamic, very quick," said MAIB principal inspector Simon Graves. "The speed of events overtook the crew and prevented them from taking any other action."

In addition to Mike Lynch, 59, the accident led to the deaths of his daughter Hannah, 18, Morgan Stanley International bank chairman Jonathan Bloomer, 70, and his wife, Judy, 71.

An American lawyer, Chris Morvillo, 59, and his wife Neda Morvillo, 57, also died, along with crew member Rick Thomas , 59.

Rob Loder, chief inspector of marine accidents said: "Our thoughts remain with the families and loved ones of the seven who lost their lives, and with all those affected by the loss of Bayesian. This accident developed with extraordinary speed."

Fifteen survivors escaped from the 56-metre (184m) luxury yacht and managed to get to a life raft that had been launched by a crew member.

The marine investigation found that the Bayesian "had a vulnerability to high winds that was not recognised, because the yacht had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down".

In addition, "the extreme winds that night were also not explicitly forecast, so the crew had no warning of the risk", Loder added.

In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

A study commissioned by the MAIB indicated that, in the conditions assessed, Bayesian was vulnerable to extreme winds at the vessels widest point, known as the beam.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

The MAIB's final report into the sinking, published on Thursday, appeared to contrast with recent reports from Italy, where prosecution experts have reportedly blamed errors by the crew rather than problems with the yacht.

The investigation was carried out alongside a criminal probe in Italy , where captain James Cutfield, chief engineer Tim Parker Eaton and deckhand Matthew Griffith are under investigation over potential charges of multiple manslaughter and culpable shipwreck.

British investigators said that Italian prosecutors had restricted access to some witnesses and evidence.

"It is possible that the circumstances depicted in this report may alter following disclosure of evidence withheld by the Italian authorities," the report says.

However, the MAIB's Graves said he was satisfied with the British investigation.

"We are content with our investigation, the investigation that we've undertaken, and the information we've used to feed into it."

The report also found that alcohol consumption had not contributed to the sinking.

The MAIB report makes seven recommendations to four agencies. It calls for new regulations to be set for single-hulled sailing vessels, and new rules around life rafts.

It also urges collaboration between the Met Office and its global counterpart to improve information-sharing of severe weather forecasts with mariners.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency is also investigating the sinking.

articles.summary: U.S. airlines are cutting seats to popular vacation destination Costa Rica this winter, with January capacity down 12.5%, and San José hit harder than Liberia as airfares climb.
articles.body: American travelers heading to a popular vacation getaway could face fewer flight options and higher airfares during the busy winter vacation season. Airlines are scheduling fewer flights and offering fewer seats from the U.S. to Costa Rica in December and January compared with last year, according to flight schedule data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company that tracks airline operations worldwide. The drop is expected to be especially noticeable after the holidays. In January, the number of available seats from the U.S. to Costa Rica is scheduled to fall 12.5% compared to a year earlier. Cirium cautioned that the booking figures do not include all reservations made directly with airlines. Airlines pull back on routes The changes follow several airline service reductions this year. JetBlue suspended service from Orlando, while Frontier paused its San José flights between August and October, according to an October report from Costa Rica's Center for Tourism Studies (CET). articles.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgence
articles.summary: Pennsylvania records eighth measles death of 2026, a day after the US formally loses its 26-year elimination status.
articles.body:
An unvaccinated resident of Pennsylvania has died after contracting measles, marking the eighth measles-related fatality in the northeastern state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) confirmed the death on Wednesday and said it had been reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

While the department did not publicly identify the individual who died, it said they were a resident of Clinton County, in the centre of the state.

The latest death comes shortly after the United States formally lost its measles elimination status, a designation it held for nearly 26 years.

That status indicated that measles was not endemic to the US, meaning no single strain had circulated continuously for 12 months or more.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) , a branch of the World Health Organization, updated the US’s designation on Tuesday after reviewing transmission data from the country.

The US is grappling with its worst measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of November 12, the CDC had counted 5,412 confirmed cases since the start of the year.

Pennsylvania, meanwhile, reported 1,589 cases across 46 of its 67 counties. The state’s health agency pledged to continue its aggressive response to the outbreak.

“Approximately 300 DOH staff are proactively working with residents, community organizations, and health care providers to combat the measles outbreak in the Commonwealth through access to fact-based information and access to the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine,” the department wrote in a news release.

The agency also said state health officials have administered more than 11,500 MMR vaccine doses in 2026, including more than 7,200 shots in pop-up clinics since the outbreak erupted in late April.

Experts say vaccine hesitancy in recent decades has contributed to the rising number of cases.

Measles is highly contagious and can spread quickly, particularly when someone coughs or sneezes. The virus can survive for up to two hours in the air, and an estimated 90 percent of those who are not immune will catch it upon exposure, according to medical authorities.

Critics point to leadership under US President Donald Trump as contributing to the measles outbreaks.

One of Trump’s cabinet officials, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has questioned the efficacy and safety of vaccines like the MMR shot.

He also said in an interview with NewsNation that the MMR vaccine “contains a lot of aborted foetus debris and DNA particles”, an unsubstantiated claim.

Still, he encouraged vaccination in a social media post on Tuesday, following PAHO’s decision to revoke the US’s measles elimination status.

“We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles,” he wrote.

The CDC also said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said.

Before taking office in early 2025, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.
